question.prompt:
When the roots of the polynomial

\[ \begin{gathered} P(x)=(x-1)^1(x-2)^2 \\ {}\cdot (x-3)^3\cdots \\ {}\cdot (x-10)^{10} \end{gathered} \]

are removed from the number line, what remains is the union of \(11\) disjoint open intervals. On how many of these intervals is \(P(x)\) positive?

solutions.title: Count negative odd factors
solutions.explanation:
Even powers are positive away from their roots, so only factors with odd exponents affect the sign of \(P(x)\).

An odd power has the same sign as its base. Thus, at every point remaining on the number line, \(P(x)\) has the same sign as
\[
Q(x)=(x-1)(x-3)(x-5)(x-7)(x-9).
\]
A factor \(x-k\) is negative exactly when \(x<k\), and a product of nonzero factors is positive exactly when it has an even number of negative factors. This gives the table below. We will account for the removed even-numbered roots afterward.

| Range of \(x\) | Number of negative factors in \(Q(x)\) | Sign of \(Q(x)\) |
|---|---:|:---:|
| \((-\infty,1)\) | 5 | \(-\) |
| \((1,3)\) | 4 | \(+\) |
| \((3,5)\) | 3 | \(-\) |
| \((5,7)\) | 2 | \(+\) |
| \((7,9)\) | 1 | \(-\) |
| \((9,\infty)\) | 0 | \(+\) |

The positive ranges are therefore \((1,3)\), \((5,7)\), and \((9,\infty)\). However, \(2,6,10\) are roots of the original polynomial and must be removed. Each splits one positive range into two of the intervals specified in the question:
\[
(1,2),\ (2,3),\ (5,6),\ (6,7),\ (9,10),\ (10,\infty).
\]
All other intervals have negative sign. Hence there are exactly \(\boxed{6}\) positive intervals, choice \(\text{C}\).
